notes.text: For more than 8, use your biggest pot, and give the onion a few extra minutes to turn golden.

move.title: Spices wake up in oil
move.body: Chana masala is a chickpea curry from North India. Today you'll cook onion until golden, wake up ground spices in the hot oil, and cook tomatoes down into a thick sauce for the chickpeas. That onion-tomato-spice base starts many Indian dishes.

why.title: Small onion pieces melt in
why.body: Small, even onion pieces cook golden at the same time and melt into the sauce. Big pieces stay chunky, and little ones burn before big ones soften.

why.title: Wake up the spices
why.body: Ground spices taste dusty from the jar. Thirty seconds in hot oil wakes up their smell and flavor. Much longer, and they burn and taste bitter, so the tomatoes go in right after.

why.title: Watch for the oil
why.body: As the tomatoes cook, their water steams away. When the sauce is thick and you see oil shining at the edges, the base is ready. Indian cooks use this sign instead of a timer.

why.title: Mash a few chickpeas
why.body: Mashing some chickpeas against the pot lets out their starch, which thickens the sauce without any flour.

wrong.fix: Add the tomatoes right away to cool the pot. Next time, have the tomatoes open and ready before the spices go in.
Mash a few more chickpeas and simmer with the lid off for 5 more minutes.
Serve theirs with a spoonful of plain yogurt on top, and plenty of rice.
Sprinkle 2 tablespoons of water over it, put the lid on, and cook on low 5 more minutes.

quiz.q: Why do the spices go into the hot oil?
choices: The oil wakes up their flavor
quiz.explain: Only for about 30 seconds, or they burn.

quiz.q: How do you know the tomato base is ready?
choices: It's thick and oil shines at the edges

quiz.q: How do you thicken the sauce?
choices: Mash some chickpeas against the pot

ingredients.prep: basmati if you can find it

steps.text: Put the rice in the colander and rinse it under cold water, swishing it with your hand, until the water runs almost clear.
steps.tip: Rinsing washes off loose starch, so the grains don't stick together.

steps.text: Put the rice and the rice's water in the saucepan. Bring it to a boil over high heat, stir once, put the lid on, and turn the heat to low.
steps.tip: Don't lift the lid while it cooks. The steam is doing the work.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half through the root and peel it, leaving the root on. Lay each half flat side down, cut strips toward the root, then cut across them to dice it small.
steps.tip: Hold the onion with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Peel the garlic and mince it. Peel the ginger with the edge of a spoon and grate it on the fine side of the grater. Put them together in the small bowl.
steps.tip: Grate the ginger slowly. The last little piece is the one that catches fingers, so stop before it gets too small.

steps.text: Measure the cumin, paprika, turmeric, and cayenne into a little pile on a plate next to the stove.
steps.tip: Spices cook in seconds, so have them measured and ready before the pot gets hot.

steps.text: Open the cans of chickpeas with the can opener. Pour them into the colander and rinse them under cold water.
When the rice timer rings, move the pot off the heat and leave the lid on until you're ready to eat.
Heat the oil in the large pot over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring now and then, until it's soft and golden.
steps.look: Soft and golden brown at the edges, with no dark burnt bits.

steps.text: Add the garlic and ginger and stir for about a minute, until you can smell them.
Add the spices and stir for 30 seconds, then pour in the tomatoes right away.
steps.tip: The tomatoes hiss when they go in. Pour them slowly, close to the pot.

steps.text: Add the salt and cook the tomatoes, stirring and scraping the bottom, until they're thick and a little oil shows at the edges.
steps.look: Thick and darker red, with shiny oil around the edges.

steps.text: Add the chickpeas and the water. Bring it to a bubble, then turn it down and simmer, stirring now and then.
Press some chickpeas against the side of the pot with the back of the spoon to mash them, and stir them in. Stir in the garam masala.
steps.look: A thick sauce that coats the spoon.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Taste a little on a clean spoon, after letting it cool, and add a pinch more salt if it needs it.
Fluff the rice with a fork. Serve the chana masala over the rice, with cilantro on top if you're using it.
steps.tip: Squeeze a little lemon over the top for a bright finish.

add.text: This recipe serves 6. Scale it to 12 on paper: double every amount. Set the servings to 12 and check your list against the app's.
add.tip: Salt and cayenne: start at about one and a half times, then taste.

add.text: Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear. Bring it to a boil with its water, cover, and cook on low. Rest it off the heat, covered.
Brunoise the onion. Mince the garlic, grate the ginger, measure the spices into one pile, and drain and rinse the chickpeas.
Soften the onion in the oil in the large pot over medium heat until golden.
Add the garlic and ginger for 1 minute, then the spices for 30 seconds, then the tomatoes and salt.
Cook down, scraping the bottom, until the oil separates at the edges.
Add the chickpeas and water and simmer. A doubled batch takes a few minutes longer to come to a simmer, not twice as long.
Mash a ladleful of chickpeas against the pot, stir in the garam masala, and adjust the salt.
add.look: A sauce that coats the spoon.

add.text: Serve over the rice with cilantro and lemon wedges.
